[descent_text] Watch for loose rock and inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully (plunge-stepping is fine on consolidated snow but the gully holds loose rock once it melts out), and take care not to cliff yourself out in the timber band by drifting off the ascent line.

routes.whyDry: Ridge snow typically cleared in season; axe only early season.
routes.quote: Snow typically cleared from the ridge
snowSentences: [gear] ice axe early season .
[what_to_bring] extra water — little reliable water source after early-season snowmelt, and post-fire slopes offer less shade .
[approach] Water is generally abundant from snowmelt streams in the lower basin (below ~4,300 ft) but can dry up by late summer;
[seasonal_guidance] Snow typically cleared from the ridge but brush and any lingering saturated lower slopes can still slow the approach .
[seasonal_hazards] N/A - no glacier travel .

routes.name: Jötnar
routes.whyDry: Snowmelt waterfalls are a spring/early-summer issue.
routes.quote: after spring snowmelt stops running down pitches 5-6
snowSentences: [hazards] High avalanche danger in winter due to maritime-influenced wet, heavy snow accumulation .
[obj_haz] rockfall from North Index and the buttress-Middle Index gully (worst in early-season snowmelt) .
[seasonal_guidance] Late July through August, after spring snowmelt stops running down pitches 5-6 and before autumn rain returns .
[seasonal_guidance] Snowmelt runs as waterfalls down pitches 5-6 and the north-facing wall stays wet, mossy and dripping, with loose rock in the water paths.
[seasonal_hazards] N/A - no glacier travel .
[best_season] Late July through early September is the optimal climbing window, chosen specifically to avoid the spring and early summer snowmelt that creates seasonal waterfalls on pitches 5-6.
[best_season] The marine west coast climate brings wet, heavy snow in winter with high avalanche danger, making winter climbing inadvisable.
[approach_variants] In early summer the lakeside traverse crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow.

routes.name: West Route
routes.whyDry: Shaded snow only before mid-July; August season is dry talus.
routes.quote: many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe before mid-July.
snowSentences: [overview] Massie Peak is a remote, seldom-visited summit on the ridge above Massie Lake in the Phelps Creek/Chiwawa River high country of the Glacier Peak Wilderness.
[gear] ice axe (early season) .
[approach] Ford the Chiwawa River at this point (can run cold and pushy with snowmelt into early summer;
[approach] Snow and ice can linger on shaded sections of the high route and ridge well into summer;
[approach] many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe for trips before mid-July.
[seasonal_guidance] lingering snow patches and higher creek crossings are likely earlier in the month .
[climbing_route] Snow and ice linger on shaded sections of the ridge well into summer;
[climbing_route] many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe before mid-July.

routes.name: Tribute to Richard
routes.whyDry: Snow only on early or late season descent slopes.
routes.quote: treacherous when snow-covered in early or late season
snowSentences: [hazards] The approach and descent cross loose talus and heather benches above Upper Eagle Lake, terrain that is slippery when wet and treacherous when snow-covered in early or late season.
[watch_out] with snow on it, or in the dark, it is more dangerous than the climb.
[what_to_bring] Ice axe if any snow lingers on the descent slopes .
[descent_text] In an early- or late-season attempt with snow on the slopes, the descent to the lake is the crux of the day rather than the climb — carry an axe.
[seasonal_guidance] Mid-July through August, once FR 4340-300 and the Eagle Lakes trail are snow-free and the East Face is dry .
[seasonal_guidance] late July brings a dry face with morning sun, early July may still have snow above Upper Eagle Lake.
[seasonal_guidance] The Crater Creek road and upper trail can still hold snow, and the upper slopes and descent stay snowy and wet.
[best_season] The route needs the East Face dry and the approach trail snow-free;

routes.name: Nothing Couloir
routes.whyDry: Late-season dry-rock couloir; route wants the snow gone.
routes.quote: This is explicitly a late-season line — it wants the snow gone and the rock dry .
snowSentences: [name] Nothing Couloir .

[overview] A late-season class 3/4 rock scramble up a clean, solid-rock couloir system on Mount Maude's WNW side, the second gully right of the North Tower, finishing along the summit ridge with brief class 4 moves around towers.
[beta] From the west side of the mountain, locate the couloir as the second gully to the right of the North Tower.
[beta] Follow the shallow right fork up slabby class 3 rock, move right into another couloir with a brief class 4 step, then continue sustained slabby class 3 climbing to the ridge crest.

[approach] Same lower approach as the North Face/Entiat Icefall routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft) via FR 6211, up the Phelps Creek Trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the climber's trail into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,100-6,200 ft, ~5 miles), continuing onto the peak's west side to reach the base of the couloir system near the standard West/South Slopes route.

[descent_text] Descend the South Shoulder route, which pairs well with the Nothing Couloir's west-side approach to form a natural loop back down toward Leroy Creek Basin rather than reversing the climb.
[bail] The moderate class 3-4 nature of the couloir makes downclimbing a reasonably straightforward retreat option at most points below the summit ridge.
[turnaround] Because the route depends on dry rock, turn back if the couloir is wet, snow-covered, or holding loose debris;

routes.name: Standard Route
routes.whyDry: Col snow only into early summer; slopes clear in season.
routes.quote: Snow or cornicing in the col into early summer .
snowSentences: [beta] Above the lake the route leaves the trail, climbing through avalanche-damaged timber to treeline near 5,800 ft, then ascending loose scree and talus -- either angling toward the roughly 6,420-ft saddle between Iron Mountain and Worthington, or straight up a wide gully south of the lake -- to the peak's open summit plateau.
[hazards] Lingering snow or cornicing in the Iron–Worthington col into early summer .
[watch_out] Snow or ice in the col even after the trail itself is snow-free .
[what_to_bring] ice axe (early season) .

[descent_text] From the base of the summit block, descend southwest back to the Iron-Worthington col, then drop into the wide scree/talus gully on the west side of the col -- this is the standout feature of the descent, offering a fast, low-angle boot-ski through loose scree and talus back down to treeline and the avalanche-debris bench above Buckhorn Lake.
[seasonal_guidance] slopes generally clear of snow with stable long days .
[seasonal_guidance] lingering snow on upper slopes typical this early in the season;
[seasonal_guidance] route-finding harder and snow travel gear likely needed .

routes.name: Pinnacle Saddle / North Slopes
routes.whyDry: Boot-path snowfield lingers into July; late July-September is snow-free.
routes.quote: Late July through September is most reliable for snow-free travel
snowSentences: [hazards] Lingering snowfield on the boot path and near the saddle well into summer, icy in early morning .
[obj_haz] lingering snow or ice on the boot path into early summer .
[gear] Microspikes or a light ice axe if attempting before mid-July .
[what_to_bring] ice axe .

[approach] around 0.5 mi you get a first partial view of Rainier through the trees, and at about 0.6 mi you cross a seasonal stream/cascading creek that is the only reliable water on the hike (dry by late summer in low-snow years).

[approach] By 0.7 mi the trail breaks out of forest into open talus and heather slopes below the cliffs of Pinnacle Peak, and steepens noticeably from here — this is where lingering snow (well into July on the shaded, north-facing switchbacks) creates the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock.
[approach] A lingering snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July — either kick steps straight up it or skirt left on the rockier tread;

[descent_text] The same hazards apply in reverse: lingering snow on the steep north-facing switchbacks just below the saddle is the most common problem spot (an ice axe or trekking poles with caution are worth carrying into July in high-snow years), and the talus sections can be slick when wet.

routes.name: Scramble Route
routes.whyDry: Snow and cornices only into June.
routes.quote: snow lingers here with cornices along the edges into June
snowSentences: [beta] The entire ridge section is exposed on both sides with uneven terrain.
[obj_haz] Lingering snow/ice or cornices on the ridge in early season, turning the scramble into technical snow travel .
[watch_out] snow coverage masks terrain.
[approach] The saddle is exposed with cliff edges that can be corniced with lingering snow into June;

[descent_text] Once back at the saddle, descend the well-graded trail switchbacks through alpine meadow (watch for exposure and uneven terrain in the saddle area—use extreme caution as falls could be deadly), then through old-growth forest.

[climbing_route] The saddle and the slopes on either side are narrow, uneven and cliffed on both sides, and snow lingers here with cornices along the edges into June — an unroped slip on frozen morning snow is the realistic accident on this peak, not a fall while rock climbing.
[climbing_route] Verify conditions before committing — the same moves are a different proposition with wet rock or old snow in the gully.
[rope_note] Winter/spring conditions call for ice axe, crampons/microspikes, and helmet due to steep upper meadow terrain with avalanche exposure.

routes.name: South Face
routes.whyDry: Notch snow clears by mid-July.
routes.quote: Mid-July through September, after seasonal snow clears the approach gullies and notch;
snowSentences: [hazards] Lingering snow across the approach and notch into July .
[seasonal_guidance] The gullies melt out through the month, but patches of hard snow can linger in the notch into mid-July and rockfall from the thaw is common.
[seasonal_guidance] Snow usually still fills the Burgundy Col gullies and the notch approach, and melting snow loosens rock in the gullies;
[seasonal_guidance] axe and crampons are needed.
[seasonal_guidance] Early snow and verglas on the upper cracks are common, and SR 20 can close after an early storm, stranding the approach.
[best_season] Mid-July through September, after seasonal snow clears the approach gullies and notch;

snowSentences: [hazards] Lingering snow/ice in approach gullies into early July .

[seasonal_guidance] Early July often still has lingering snowfields on approach and gullies;
[seasonal_guidance] Snow typically still covers the Royal Basin approach and Needles scramble terrain;
[seasonal_guidance] outside the best-season window and adds serious snow-travel/routefinding hazard on already-loose rock.
[seasonal_guidance] driest, most snow-free conditions for the Class 3-4 scrambling and lowest added risk from snow on top of the already-loose rock.
[seasonal_guidance] early snow and storm systems become common in the Olympics, adding avalanche/snow hazard atop the existing loose-rock and exposure hazards.
[seasonal_hazards] N/A - no glacier travel .

routes.name: Direct South Buttress
routes.whyDry: Axe and crampons only for early season or snowy years.
routes.quote: needed on the ascent and descent in early season or snowy years .
snowSentences: [what_to_bring] ice axe and crampons — needed on the ascent and descent in early season or snowy years .
[descent_text] With a single rope you can instead follow the crest west to the end of the long horizontal section and take the couloirs that drop west toward the drainage between Moran and Thor Peak.
[descent_text] Early in the season an ice axe and crampons are useful.
